newsitem.title: MEXICO: Bancomer past-due loans a problem - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bancomer past-due loans a problem - analysts.

text.p: Grupo Financiero Bancomer's 1996 results closely resembled those of larger rival Banamex-Accival, suggesting past-due loans are a problem system-wide, not just at Banamex, analysts said on Monday.
Banking group Bancomer, Mexico's second largest, reported a 448 million peso profit in 1996 versus 505 million pesos in 1995, and a 1.015 billion gain in the final quarter of 1996.
Analysts shrugged off the profit, which was considered largely window dressing, and focused on the asset quality and reserve coverage of the bank instead.

They said slightly unfavorable comparisons with Banamex on the level of loan loss reserves and asset quality estimated under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles may have caused the drop in Bancomer's shares since the report was released.
Its B shares at midday Monday were off 1.75 percent at 2.81. They closed down 2.05 percent to 2.86 pesos on Friday.
Bancomer estimated its reserve coverage under U.S. GAAP at 57.5 percent, short of Banamex's level of 61.0 percent when the new accounting is applied in the first quarter.

"The only different things (between the two banks) were that Bancomer was less conservative than Banamex in reserve coverage, and that Bancomer placed some mortgages under the 'rent' program," said Susana Ornelas, bank analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.

In using the rent program, in which properties with unpaid mortgages are returned to the bank and rented to their occupants instead, analysts said Bancomer managed to keep some one billion pesos of mortgage loans out of past-due status, a practice Banamex avoided.

In terms of asset quality, she said, in general the past-due loan ratios were similar, though in the mortgage category, past-due loans grew 410 percent at Bancomer when U.S. GAAP is applied. At Banamex, they were up 236 percent.

The rise in Banamex bad loans stunned analysts last week, but after Bancomer's report, they pointed out that the problem appeared to be general. "It's more of a system-wide issue rather than bank specific," Ornelas said.

Rogelio Urrutia, bank analyst at Valores Finamex, said the difference in reserve coverage of the two banks was fairly negligible, and in both cases they were well above the 45 percent minimum required by law under U.S. GAAP.
"I wouldn't give a premium to one over the other; the two banks were very much in line," he said.

Robert Lacoursiere of Santander Investments in Mexico City said Bancomer's net interest margins were slightly more positive than Banamex's, though they dropped an average 70 basis points quarter over quarter.

He said core deposits were up by 24 percent in the fourth quarter compared with the previous three-month period, which showed the bank was responding to pressure from fast-growing banks like Bital and BBV Probursa
On asset quality, he said there was not a lot seperating the two banks.
"I would say they're both in line. The reason why I would say Bancomer has a worse asset quality portfolio is that they did more restructuring of loans in general."

Alberto Sanchez, bank analyst at Bear Stearns, set the market talking on Monday when he downgraded Bancomer, due to what he called "higher than expected asset quality problems and a shrinking net interest margin."

He particularly pointed to the rise in past-due mortgages as a reason for singling out Bancomer for punishment. But other analysts said both banks put in such similar performances in general that they wondered why he had not cut Banacci as well.
